label: Failure to Clearly and Expressly Advise of Right to an Independent Chemical Test

trigger.description: Ask whenever the defendant was arrested for DUI and asked to submit to a breath test, to determine whether police clearly and expressly advised them of the right to an independent chemical test.

review_conditions.display_note: Whether an advisement was clear and express enough is fact-specific — document exactly what was said. Note that the state, not the defendant, may choose which type of independent test to offer (Velarde v. State, 353 P.3d 355 (Alaska App. 2015)), so an incomplete list of test options isn't itself a defect — focus on whether the right itself, and the process for the test actually offered, were clearly conveyed.
Because a breath test was administered here, the remedy for this violation is suppression of that test result.

Because no breath test was administered, suppression is not a meaningful remedy — instead, seek a presumption that an independent test would have yielded a favorable result (a BAC of .04 or below). Nelson v. State, 512 P.3d 86, 90-91 (Alaska App. 2022), applying Snyder v. State, 930 P.2d 1274, 1278-79 (Alaska 1996).

excluded_explanations.display_note: Failure to Advise of Independent Test Right was considered but not included: the advisement was otherwise clear, and the only complaint is that the officer explained just one type of test (e.g. blood) without mentioning alternatives. Alaska law gives the state, not the defendant, the choice of which type of independent test to offer — this alone is not a violation. See Velarde v. State, 353 P.3d 355 (Alaska App. 2015).

rule_statements.text: The person who administers a chemical test must clearly and expressly inform the person tested of the right to an independent chemical test, and make reasonable, good-faith efforts to assist the person in obtaining one if requested.

This requirement also rests on an independent due process basis: a defendant must be given clear and express notice of the right to an independent test, because due process requires an opportunity to challenge the reliability of a state-administered chemical test in the simplest and most effective way possible.
A waiver of this right is valid only if it is knowing and intelligent.
Where a breath test was administered and is in evidence, the remedy for a violation of this right is suppression of that test result.
Where no breath test exists to suppress, the fact-finder must instead presume that an independent test, had one been conducted, would have yielded a favorable result.

practice_notes: Determine early whether a breath test was actually administered and is in evidence — the available remedy differs sharply: suppression of an existing test, versus a favorable-BAC presumption if none exists. Don't assume suppression is available in every case.

The state, not the defendant, gets to choose which type of independent test to offer (e.g. blood vs. breath) — an incomplete explanation of alternatives isn't itself a violation. Focus on whether the right itself, and the offered test's process, were clearly conveyed.

This overlaps closely with the comprehension-barrier issue — if the advisement was properly given but the defendant couldn't understand it (language, intoxication), that's a different issue resting on different facts, not this one.
